Who Will Ride the New Lines?

Ridership and access for the Jurong Region Line and Cross Island Line

Author

Hung · ISSS626 Take-home Exercise 3 · Executive Summary

Published

November 13, 2026

  2. Study area and data

Slides with charts have tabs above the chart: click a tab to see more evidence from the technical report.

Research question

Singapore is building the Jurong Region Line (24 stations) and Cross Island Line Phase 1 (12 stations). Before they open, planners need to know:

  • Which new stations will be busy, and which may be quiet?
  • Which existing stations will lose riders to them?
  • Which neighbourhoods get real walking access to rail?

36proposed stations

29new places to board

7existing stations that gain a line

Study area and data

  • Network
  • Where people live
  • Where people work
  • Homes vs workplaces
  • Today’s entries
  • Passenger volumes from LTA DataMall, Aug–Sep 2026: 3,086,450 entries on an average weekday at 184 open stations
  • Station and bus stop locations from LTA, Sep 2026
  • Future station coordinates from an open-source dataset
  • 13,436 HDB buildings from data.gov.sg
  • Subzones, workplaces, shops and schools from OpenStreetMap

Homes and workplaces sit in different places, so both are modelled as places where trips start.

Analytical approach

A Huff model: riders at each place choose among stations by distance and attractiveness.

1. Where trips start

  • 13,436 HDB buildings, weighted by footprint
  • Workplace and activity locations in 500 m cells

2. What makes a station attractive

  • Number of lines
  • MRT versus LRT-only
  • Bus stops within 400, 500 or 800 m, roughly 5- and 10-minute walks. The best-fitting radius is kept.

3. Calibrate, test, apply

  • Fit distance decay and attraction to observed entries
  • Test on five geographic groups of stations the model has not seen
  • Apply to four networks: today, +JRL, +CRL, both

The model shares today’s trips out among stations. It does not add riders from future housing or from people switching from buses and cars.

How well the model works

  • Error by model
  • Observed vs predicted
  • Bias by type
  • Stability
  • Distance decay
  • CBD vs neighbourhood

38.2%error on stations the model has not seen, against 80.7% using distance alone

  • Knowing where people work matters as much as knowing where they live.
  • The model is weakest in the city centre. Raffles Place peaks at the evening commute, and many of its riders come from outside the modelled demand.
  • Distance decay barely moves across the test folds. Bus stops add little.

Ridership at the new stations

  • Predicted entries
  • Distance to existing
  • Bus stops nearby

9.0%of weekday entries move to the 29 new stations

  • The busiest are Serangoon North (CR9), Tampines North (CR6), Pasir Ris East (CR4), all on the CRL and next to large HDB estates.
  • Nanyang Gateway (JW3) and Tengah (JS3) may be quiet, with under 4,800 entries a day. That is the level of the quietest tenth of today’s MRT stations.
  • New stations have fewer bus stops nearby today. Feeder routes usually follow a new line.

Effects on existing stations

  • Biggest changes
  • Biggest losses
  • By line
  • Interchange uplift
  • Catchment map
  • The biggest losses are at Pioneer (EW28), Lakeside (EW26), DT32-EW2. Most losing stations sit on the western East–West Line, next to the JRL.
  • Stations that gain a CRL platform gain the most, led by Hougang (+31%).
  • The Interchange uplift tab shows how much of that gain rests on one assumption: that an extra line attracts riders.
  • The Catchment map shows which subzones switch their preferred station. Hover over a subzone for details.

Who gets closer to a station

  • By planning area
  • Distance curves
  • Saving by line
  • Saving map

73% → 83%of HDB footprint within 800 m of a station

  • 2,111 HDB blocks get closer to a station, mostly along the two new lines.
  • Tengah gains most, going from almost no housing within 800 m of a station to most of it.
  • Still far from rail: Yishun East, Tampines West, Tampines North.

Public-safety implications

Crowding at new interchanges

Hougang’s predicted weekday entries rise from 36,700 to 47,900. At today’s peak share, its busiest hour (08:00) would see about 7,400 entries, before counting riders changing lines. Platform and concourse capacity should be checked against this.

Quiet stations

Nanyang Gateway (JW3) and Tengah (JS3) are predicted to see few riders. Low footfall means fewer people around at off-peak hours, so lighting, CCTV coverage and staffing need attention from the start.

Walking access and disruption

Estates that remain beyond 800 m, such as Yishun East and Tampines West, rely on long walks or feeder buses. Safe crossings on walking routes, and bus bridging plans for rail disruptions, matter most there.

Limitations

  • The total number of trips is fixed. The model moves today’s trips between stations, so it cannot add riders from new housing such as Tengah, or from people leaving buses and cars.
  • Distances are straight lines. Real walks are longer, and expressways, rivers and fences can make a nearby station hard to reach.
  • Homes are weighted by HDB building footprint, not by residents, and workplaces come from OpenStreetMap, whose coverage varies.
  • Only entries are modelled. Transfers inside the network are not, so crowding at interchanges is understated.
  • With no age data, effects on older residents could not be tested.
  • City-centre stations are under-predicted, because many of their riders come from outside the modelled demand.

Recommendations

  1. Gather local evidence on future housing and jobs for the quiet stations (Nanyang Gateway (JW3), Tengah (JS3)) before fixing service levels and opening dates.
  2. Review feeder buses around the stations that lose riders (Pioneer (EW28), Lakeside (EW26), DT32-EW2), so routes follow riders to the new lines.
  3. Check capacity and safety at the new interchanges, starting with Hougang, using transfer counts as well as entries.
  4. Improve walking routes and feeder links for estates that stay beyond 800 m of a station, such as Yishun East, Tampines West, Tampines North.
